entries.41a4735e974d1ce4de729314dce045d92127ecd4: <div sID="gen20242" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="9" osisID="Amos.9" sID="Amos.9"/> <div eID="gen20242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20243" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20244" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. Judgment threatened, which the sinners shall not escape (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.1-Amos.9.4">ver. 1-4</reference>), which an almighty power shall inflict (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.5-Amos.9.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>), which the people of Israel have deserved as a sinful people (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.7-Amos.9.8">ver. 7, 8</reference>); and yet it shall not be the utter ruin of their nation (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.8">ver. 8</reference>), for a remnant of good people shall escape, <reference osisRef="Amos.9.9">ver. 9</reference>. But the wicked ones shall perish, <reference osisRef="Amos.9.10">ver. 10</reference>. II. Mercy promised, which was to be bestowed in the latter days (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.11-Amos.9.15">ver. 11-15</reference>), as appears by the application of it to the days of the Messiah, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.16">Acts xv. 16</reference>. And with those comfortable promises, after all the foregoing rebukes and threatenings, the book concludes.
entries.e4f1a9279cfe0a922ca7f14befc1abcb4d064e6b: <div eID="gen20244" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20243" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Certainty of the Sinner's Doom. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 784.)</title> <div sID="gen20245" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> I saw the Lord standing upon the altar: and he said, Smite the lintel of the door, that the posts may shake: and cut them in the head, all of them; and I will slay the last of them with the sword: he that fleeth of them shall not flee away, and he that escapeth of them shall not be delivered. <hi type="super">2</hi> Though they dig into hell, thence shall mine hand take them; though they climb up to heaven, thence will I bring them down: <hi type="super">3</hi> And though they hide themselves in the top of Carmel, I will search and take them out thence; and though they be hid from my sight in the bottom of the sea, thence will I command the serpent, and he shall bite them: <hi type="super">4</hi> And though they go into captivity before their enemies, thence will I command the sword, and it shall slay them: and I will set mine eyes upon them for evil, and not for good. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> of hosts <hi type="italic">is</hi> he that toucheth the land, and it shall melt, and all that dwell therein shall mourn: and it shall rise up wholly like a flood; and shall be drowned, as <hi type="italic">by</hi> the flood of Egypt. <hi type="super">6</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> he that buildeth his stories in the heaven, and hath founded his troop in the earth; he that calleth for the waters of the sea, and poureth them out upon the face of the earth: The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> his name. <hi type="super">7</hi> <hi type="italic">Are</hi> ye not as children of the Ethiopians unto me, O children of Israel? saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . Have not I brought up Israel out of the land of Egypt? and the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir? <hi type="super">8</hi> Behold, the eyes of the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> <hi type="italic">are</hi> upon the sinful kingdom, and I will destroy it from off the face of the earth; saving that I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">9</hi> For, lo, I will command, and I will sift the house of Israel among all nations, like as <hi type="italic">corn</hi> is sifted in a sieve, yet shall not the least grain fall upon the earth. <hi type="super">10</hi> All the sinners of my people shall die by the sword, which say, The evil shall not overtake nor prevent us. <div eID="gen20245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20246" type="x-p"/> We have here the justice of God passing sentence upon a provoking people; and observe, <div eID="gen20246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20247" type="x-p"/> I. With what solemnity the sentence is passed. The prophet saw in vision <hi type="italic">the Lord standing upon the altar</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.1">v. 1</reference>), the altar of burnt-offerings; for the <hi type="italic">Lord has a sacrifice,</hi> and multitudes must fall as victims to his justice. He is removed from the <hi type="italic">mercy-seat</hi> between the <hi type="italic">cherubim,</hi> and stands upon <hi type="italic">the altar,</hi> the <hi type="italic">judgment-seat,</hi> on which the fire of God used to fall, to devour the sacrifices. He stands upon <hi type="italic">the altar,</hi> to show that the ground of his controversy with this people was their profanation of his holy things; here he stands to avenge the quarrel of his altar, as also to signify that the sin of the house of Israel, like that of the house of Eli, shall <hi type="italic">not be purged with sacrifice nor offering forever,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.14">1 Sam. iii. 14</reference>. He stands on the altar, to prohibit sacrifice. Now the order given is, <hi type="italic">Smite the lintel of the door</hi> of the temple, the chapiter, smite it with such a blow <hi type="italic">that the posts may shake,</hi> and <hi type="italic">cut them,</hi> wound them <hi type="italic">in the head, all of them;</hi> break down the doors of God's house, or of the courts of his house, in token of this, that he is going out from it, and forsaking it, and then all judgments are breaking in upon it. Or it signifies the destruction of those in the first place that should be as the door-posts to the nation for its defence, so that, they being broken down, it becomes as a <hi type="italic">city without gates and bars.</hi> "Smite the king, who is as the lintel of the door, that the princes, who are as <hi type="italic">the posts,</hi> may <hi type="italic">shake; cut them in the head,</hi> cleave them down, <hi type="italic">all of them,</hi> as wood for the fire; and <hi type="italic">I will slay the last of them,</hi> the posterity of them, them and their families, or the <hi type="italic">least</hi> of them, them and all that are employed under them; or, I will <hi type="italic">slay them all,</hi> them and all that remain of them, till it comes to the last man; the slaughter shall be general." There is no living for those on whom God has said, <hi type="italic">I will slay</hi> them, no standing before his sword. <div eID="gen20247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20248" type="x-p"/> II. What effectual care is taken that none shall escape the execution of this sentence. This is enlarged upon here, and is intended for warning to all that <hi type="italic">provoke the Lord to jealousy.</hi> Let sinners read it, and tremble; as there is no fighting it out with God, so there is no fleeing from him. His judgments, when they come with commission, as they will overpower the strongest that think to outface them, so they will overtake the swiftest that think to out-run them, <reference osisRef="Amos.9.2">v. 2</reference>. Those of them that flee, and take to their heels, shall soon be out of breath, and shall not flee away out of the reach of danger; for, as sometimes <hi type="italic">the wicked flee when none pursues,</hi> so he cannot flee away when God pursues, though <hi type="italic">he would fain flee out of his hand.</hi> Nay, <hi type="italic">he that escapes of them,</hi> that thinks he has gained his point, <hi type="italic">shall not be delivered. Evil pursues sinners,</hi> and will arrest them. This is here enlarged upon by showing that wherever sinners flee for shelter from God's justice, it will overtake them, and the shelter will prove but a <hi type="italic">refuge of lies.</hi> What David says of the ubiquity of God's presence ( <reference osisRef="Ps.139.7-Ps.139.10">Ps. cxxxix. 7-10</reference>) is here said of the extent of God's power and justice. (1.) Hell itself, though it has its name in English from its being <hi type="italic">hilled,</hi> or <hi type="italic">covered over,</hi> or <hi type="italic">hidden,</hi> cannot hide them (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.2">v. 2</reference>): "Though <hi type="italic">they dig into hell,</hi> into the centre of the earth, or the darkest recesses of it, yet <hi type="italic">thence shall my hand take them,</hi> and bring them forth to be made public monuments of divine justice." The grave is a hiding-place to the righteous from the malice of the world (<reference osisRef="Job.3.17">Job iii. 17</reference>), but it shall be no hiding-place to the righteous from the justice of God; thence God's hands shall take them, when they shall rise in the great day to <hi type="italic">everlasting shame and contempt.</hi> (2.) Heaven, though it has its name from being <hi type="italic">heaved,</hi> or lifted up, shall not put them out of reach of God's judgments; as hell cannot hide them, so heaven will not. Though they <hi type="italic">climb up to heaven</hi> in their conceit, yet <hi type="italic">thence will I bring them down.</hi> Those whom God brings to heaven by his grace shall never be brought down; but those who climb thither themselves, by their own presumption, and confidence in themselves, will be brought down and filled with shame. (3.) <hi type="italic">The top of Carmel,</hi> one of the highest parts of the dust of the world in that country, shall not protect them: "<hi type="italic">Though they hide themselves there,</hi> where they imagine nobody will look for them, <hi type="italic">I will search, and take them out thence;</hi> neither the thickest bushes, nor the darkest caves, in the <hi type="italic">top of Carmel,</hi> will serve to hide them." (4.) The <hi type="italic">bottom of the sea</hi> shall not serve to conceal them; though they think to hide themselves there, even there the judgments of God shall find them out, and lay hold on them: <hi type="italic">Thence will I command the serpent, and he shall bite them,</hi> the <hi type="italic">crooked serpent,</hi> even <hi type="italic">the dragon that is in the sea,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Isa. xxvii. 1</reference>. They shall find their plague and death where they hope to find shelter and protection; diving will stand them in no more stead than climbing. (5.) Remote countries will not befriend them, nor shall less judgments excuse them from greater (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thought they go into captivity before their enemies,</hi> who carry them to places at a great distance, and mingle them with their own people, among whom they seem to be lost, yet that shall not serve their turn: <hi type="italic">Thence will I command the sword, and it shall slay them,</hi> the sword of the enemy, or one another's sword. When God judges he will overcome. That which binds on all this, makes their escape impossible and their ruin inevitable, is that God will <hi type="italic">set his eyes upon them for evil, and not for good.</hi> His eyes are in every place, are upon all men and upon all the ways of men, upon some for good, to <hi type="italic">show himself strong</hi> on their behalf, but upon others for evil, to take notice of their sins (<reference osisRef="Job.13.27">Job xiii. 27</reference>) and take all opportunities of punishing them for their sins. <hi type="italic">Their</hi> case is truly miserable who have the providence of God: and all the dispensations of it, against them, working for their hurt. <div eID="gen20248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20249" type="x-p"/> 3. What a great and mighty God he is that passes this sentence upon them, and will take the executing of it into his own hands. Threatenings are more or less formidable according to the power of him that threatens. We laugh at impotent wrath; but the wrath of God is not so; it is omnipotent wrath. <hi type="italic">Who knows the power</hi> of it? What he had before said he would do (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.8">ch. viii. 8</reference>) is here repeated, that he would <hi type="italic">make the land melt</hi> and tremble, and <hi type="italic">all that dwell therein mourn,</hi> that the judgment should <hi type="italic">rise up wholly like a flood,</hi> and the country should be <hi type="italic">drowned,</hi> and laid under water, <hi type="italic">as by the flood of Egypt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.9.5">v. 5</reference>. But is he able to make his words good? Yes, certainly he is; he does but <hi type="italic">touch the land</hi> and <hi type="italic">it melts, touch the mountains</hi> and they smoke; he can do it with the greatest ease, for, (1.) He is <hi type="italic">the Lord God of hosts,</hi> who undertakes to do it, the God who has all the power in his hand, and all creatures at his beck and call, who having made them all, and given them their several capacities, makes what use he pleases of them and all their powers. Very miserable is the case of those who have the Lord of hosts against them, for they have hosts against them, the whole creation at war with them. (2.) He is the Creator and governor of the upper world: <hi type="italic">It is he that builds his stories in the heavens,</hi> the celestial orbs, or spheres, one over another, as so many stories in a high and stately palace. They are his, for he built them at first, when he said, <hi type="italic">Let there be a firmament, and he made the firmament;</hi> and he builds them still, is continually building them, not that they need repair, but by his providence he still upholds them; his power is the pillars of heaven, by which it is borne up. Now he that has the command of those stories is certainly to be feared, for thence, as from a castle, he can fire upon his enemies, or cast upon them great hailstones, as on the Canaanites, or make the stars in their courses, the furniture of those stories, to fight against them, as against Sisera. (3.) He has the management and command of this lower world too, in which we dwell, the terraqueous globe, both <hi type="italic">earth</hi> and <hi type="italic">sea,</hi> so that, which way soever his enemies think to make their escape, he will meet them, or to make opposition, he will match them. Do they think to make a land-fight of it? He <hi type="italic">has founded his troop in the earth,</hi> his troop of guards, which he has at command, and makes use of for the protection of his subjects and the punishment of his enemies. All the creatures on earth make one bundle (as the margin reads it), one bundle of arrows, out of which he takes what he pleases to discharge against the persecutors, <reference osisRef="Ps.7.13">Ps. vii. 13</reference>. They are all one <hi type="italic">army,</hi> one <hi type="italic">body,</hi> so closely are they connected, and so harmoniously and so much in concert do they act for the accomplishing of their Creator's purposes. Do they think to make a sea-fight of it? He will be too hard for them there, for he has the waters of the sea at command; even its waves, the most tumultuous rebellious waters, do obey him. He <hi type="italic">calls for the waters of the sea</hi> in the course of his common providence, <hi type="italic">causes vapours to ascend</hi> out of it, and <hi type="italic">pours them out</hi> in showers, the small rain and the great rain of his strength, <hi type="italic">upon the face of the earth;</hi> this was mentioned before as a reason why we should <hi type="italic">seek the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.8">ch. v. 8</reference>) and make him our friend, as it is here made a reason why we should fear him and dread having him for our enemy. <div eID="gen20249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20250" type="x-p"/> 4. How justly God passes this sentence upon the people of Israel. He does not destroy them by an act of sovereignty, but by an act of righteousness; for (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.8">v. 8</reference>), it is a <hi type="italic">sinful kingdom,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">eyes of the Lord</hi> are upon it, discovering it to be so; he sees the great sinfulness of it, and therefore he will <hi type="italic">destroy it from off the face of the earth.</hi> Note, When those kingdoms that in name and profession were holy kingdoms, and kingdoms of priests, as Israel was, become sinful kingdoms, no other can be expected than that they should be cut off and abandoned. Let sinful kingdoms, and sinful families, and sinful persons too, see the eyes of the Lord upon them, observing all their wickedness, and reserving the notice of it for the day of reckoning and recompence. This being a sinful kingdom, see how light God makes of it, <reference osisRef="Amos.9.7">v. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen20250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20251" type="x-p"/> (1.) Of the relation wherein he stood to it: <hi type="italic">Are you not as children of Ethiopians unto me, O children of Israel?</hi> A sad change! Children of Israel become as children of the Ethiopians! [1.] They were so in themselves; that was their sin. It is a thing to be greatly lamented that the children of Israel often become as children of the Ethiopians; this children of godly parents degenerate, and become the reverse of those that went before them. Those that were well-educated, and trained up in the knowledge and fear of God, and set out well, and promised fair, throw off their profession and become as bad as the worst. <hi type="italic">How has the gold become dim!</hi> [2.] They were so in God's account, and that was their punishment. He valued them no more, though they were children of Israel, than if they had been <hi type="italic">children of the Ethiopians.</hi> We read of one in the title of <reference osisRef="Ps.7.1-Ps.7.17">Ps. vii.</reference> that was <hi type="italic">Cush</hi> (an <hi type="italic">Ethiopian,</hi> as some understand it) and yet a Benjamite. Those that by birth and profession are children of Israel, if they degenerate, and become wicked and vile, are to God no more than children of the Ethiopians. This is an intimation of the rejection of the unbelieving Jews in the days of the Messiah; because they embraced not the doctrine of Christ, the kingdom of God was taken from them, they were unchurched, and cast out of covenant, became as children of the Ethiopians, and are so to this day. And it is true of those that are called Christians, but do not live up to their name and profession, that rest in the form of piety, but live under the power of reigning iniquity, that they are to God as children of the Ethiopians; he rejects them, and their services. <div eID="gen20251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20252" type="x-p"/> (2.) See how light he makes of the favours he had conferred upon them; they thought he would not, he could not, cast them off, and put them upon a level with other nations, because he had done that for them which he had not done for other nations, whereby they thought he was bound to them, so as never to leave them. "No," says he, "The favours shown to you are not so distinguishing as you think they are: <hi type="italic">Have I not brought up Israel out of the land of Egypt?</hi>" It is true I have; but I have also brought the <hi type="italic">Philistines from Caphtor,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Cappadocia,</hi> where they were natives, or captives, or both; they are called the <hi type="italic">remnant of the country of Caphtor</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.47.4">Jer. xlvii. 4</reference>), and the Philistim are joined with the Caphtorim, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.14">Gen. x. 14</reference>. In like manner the Syrians were brought up from Kir when they had been carried away thither, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.9">2 Kings xvi. 9</reference>. Note, If God's Israel lose the peculiarity of their holiness, they lose the peculiarity of their privileges; and what was designed as a favour of special grace shall be set in another light, shall have its property altered, and shall become an act of <hi type="italic">common providence;</hi> if professors liken themselves to the world, God will level them with the world. And, if we live not up to the obligation of God's mercies, we forfeit the honour and comfort of them. <div eID="gen20252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20253" type="x-p"/> 5. How graciously God will separate between the precious and the vile in the day of retribution. Though the wicked Israelites shall be as the wicked Ethiopians, and their being called Israelites shall stand them in no stead, yet the pious Israelites shall not be as the <hi type="italic">wicked</hi> ones; no, the <hi type="italic">Judge of all the earth will do right,</hi> more right than to <hi type="italic">slay the righteous with the wicked,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.18.25">Gen. xviii. 25</reference>. His <hi type="italic">eyes are upon the sinful kingdom,</hi> to spy out those in it who preserve their integrity and swim against the stream, who sigh and cry for the abominations of their land, and they shall be marked for preservation, so that the destruction shall not be total: <hi type="italic">I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob,</hi> not ruin them by wholesale and in the gross, good and bad together, but I will distinguish, as becomes a righteous judge. The house of Israel shall be <hi type="italic">sifted as corn is sifted;</hi> they shall be greatly hurried, and shaken, and tossed, but still in the hands of God, in both his hands, as the sieve in the hands of him that sifts (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will sift the house of Israel among all nations.</hi> Wherever they are shaken and scattered, God will have his eye upon them, and will take care to separate between the corn and chaff, which was the thing he designed in sifting them. (1.) The righteous ones among them, that are as the solid wheat, shall none of them perish; they shall be delivered either from or through the common calamities of the kingdom; <hi type="italic">not the least grain shall fall on the earth,</hi> so as to be lost and forgotten—not the least <hi type="italic">stone</hi> (so the word is), for the good corn is weighty as a stone in comparison with that which we call <hi type="italic">light corn.</hi> Note, Whatever shakings there may be in the world, God does and will effectually provide that none who are truly his shall be truly miserable. (2.) The wicked ones among them who are hardened in their sins shall all of them perish, <reference osisRef="Amos.9.10">v. 10</reference>. See what a height of impiety they have come to: <hi type="italic">They say, The evil shall not overtake nor prevent us.</hi> They think they are innocent, and do not deserve punishment, or that the profession they make of relation to God will be their exemption and security from punishment, or that they shall be able to make their part good against the judgments of God, that they shall flee so swiftly from them that they shall not overtake them, or guard so carefully against them that they shall not prevent or surprise them. Note, Hope of impunity is the deceitful refuge of the impenitent. But see what it will come to at last: <hi type="italic">All the sinners</hi> that thus flatter themselves, and affront God, shall <hi type="italic">die by the sword,</hi> the sword of war, which to them shall be the sword of divine vengeance; yea, though they be the <hi type="italic">sinners of my people,</hi> for their profession shall not be their protection. Note, Evil is often nearest those that put it at the greatest distance from them.
entries.6333e72920728155212875aa3c93ad154231eb81: <div eID="gen20253" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Promises of Mercy. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 784.)</title> <div sID="gen20254" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof; and I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old: <hi type="super">12</hi> That they may possess the remnant of Edom, and of all the heathen, which are called by my name, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that doeth this. <hi type="super">13</hi> Behold, the days come, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the treader of grapes him that soweth seed; and the mountains shall drop sweet wine, and all the hills shall melt. <hi type="super">14</hi> And I will bring again the captivity of my people of Israel, and they shall build the waste cities, and inhabit <hi type="italic">them;</hi> and they shall plant vineyards, and drink the wine thereof; they shall also make gardens, and eat the fruit of them. <hi type="super">15</hi> And I will plant them upon their land, and they shall no more be pulled up out of their land which I have given them, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God. <div eID="gen20254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20255" type="x-p"/> To him to whom all the prophets bear witness this prophet, here in the close, bears his testimony, and speaks of <hi type="italic">that day,</hi> those days that shall come, in which God will do great things for his church, by the setting up of the kingdom of the Messiah, for the rejecting of which the rejection of the Jews was foretold in the <reference osisRef="Amos.9.1-Amos.9.10">foregoing verses</reference>. The promise here is said to agree to the planting of the Christian church, and in that to be fulfilled, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.15-Acts.15.17">Acts xv. 15-17</reference>. It is promised, <div eID="gen20255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20256" type="x-p"/> I. That in the Messiah the kingdom of David shall be restored (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.11">v. 11</reference>); the <hi type="italic">tabernacle of David</hi> it is called, that is, his house and family, which, though great and fixed, yet, in comparison with the kingdom of heaven, was mean and movable as a tabernacle. The church militant, in its present state, dwelling as in shepherds' tents to feed, as in soldiers' tents to fight, is the <hi type="italic">tabernacle of David.</hi> God's tabernacle is called the tabernacle of David because David desired and chose to <hi type="italic">dwell in God's tabernacle for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.61.4">Ps. lxi. 4</reference>. Now, 1. These tabernacles had fallen and gone to decay, the royal family was so impoverished, its power abridged, its honour stained, and laid in the dust; for many of that race degenerated, and in the captivity it lost the imperial dignity. Sore breaches were made upon it, and at length it was laid in ruins. So it was with the church of the Jews; in the latter days of it its glory departed; it was like a tabernacle broken down and brought to ruin, in respect both of purity and of prosperity. 2. By Jesus Christ these tabernacles were raised and rebuilt. In him God's covenant with David had its accomplishment; and the glory of that house, which was not only sullied, but quite sunk, revived again; the <hi type="italic">breaches</hi> of it were <hi type="italic">closed</hi> and its <hi type="italic">ruins raised up, as in the days of old;</hi> nay, the spiritual glory of the family of Christ far exceeded the temporal glory of the family of David when it was at its height. In him also God's covenant with Israel had its accomplishment, and in the gospel-church the tabernacle of God was set up among men again, and raised up out of the ruins of the Jewish state. This is quoted in the first council at Jerusalem as referring to the calling in of the Gentiles and God's <hi type="italic">taking out of them a people for his name.</hi> Note, While the world stands God will have a church in it, and, if it be fallen down in one place and among one people, it shall be raised up elsewhere. <div eID="gen20256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20257" type="x-p"/> II. That that kingdom shall be enlarged, and the territories of it shall extend far, by the accession of many countries to it (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.12">v. 12</reference>), that the house of David may possess the <hi type="italic">remnant of Edom, and of all the heathen,</hi> that is, that Christ may have them given him for his <hi type="italic">inheritance,</hi> even the <hi type="italic">uttermost parts of the earth for his possession,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.8">Ps. ii. 8</reference>. Those that had been strangers and enemies shall become willing faithful subjects to the Son of David, shall be <hi type="italic">added to the church,</hi> or those of them that are <hi type="italic">called by my name, saith the Lord,</hi> that is, that belong to the election of grace and are ordained to eternal life (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.48">Acts xiii. 48</reference>), for it is true of the Gentiles as well as of the Jews that <hi type="italic">the election hath obtained</hi> and <hi type="italic">the rest were blinded,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.7">Rom. xi. 7</reference>. Christ died <hi type="italic">to gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad,</hi> here said to be those that were <hi type="italic">called by his name.</hi> The promise is to all that are <hi type="italic">afar off,</hi> even as <hi type="italic">many</hi> of them <hi type="italic">as the Lord our God shall call,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.39">Acts ii. 39</reference>. St. James expounds this as a promise <hi type="italic">that the residue of men should seek after the Lord, even all the Gentiles upon whom my name is called.</hi> But may the promise be depended upon? Yes, the Lord says this, who does this, who can do it, who has determined to do it, the power of whose grace is engaged for the doing of it, and with whom saying and doing are not two things, as they are with us. <div eID="gen20257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20258" type="x-p"/> III. That in the kingdom of the Messiah there shall be great plenty, an abundance of all good things that the country produces (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">The ploughman shall overtake the reaper,</hi> that is, there shall be such a plentiful harvest every year, and so much corn to be gathered in, that it shall last all summer, even till autumn, when it is time to begin to plough again; and in like manner the vintage shall continue till seed-time, and there shall be such abundance of grapes that even the <hi type="italic">mountains shall drop new wine</hi> into the vessels of the grape-gatherers, and the hills that were dry and barren shall be moistened and shall melt with the <hi type="italic">fatness</hi> or <hi type="italic">mellowness</hi> (as we call it) <hi type="italic">of the soil.</hi> Compare this with <reference osisRef="Joel.2.24">Joel ii. 24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joel.3.18">and iii. 18</reference>. This must certainly be understood of the abundance of spiritual blessings in heavenly things, which all those are, and shall be, blessed with, who are in sincerity added to Christ and his church; they shall be abundantly replenished with the goodness of God's house, with the graces and comforts of his Spirit; they shall have bread, the bread of life, to <hi type="italic">strengthen their hearts,</hi> and the wine of divine consolations to <hi type="italic">make them glad-meat indeed</hi> and <hi type="italic">drink indeed</hi>—all the benefit that comes to the souls of men from the word and Spirit of God. These had been long confined to the vineyard of the Jewish church; divine revelation, and the power that attended it, were to be found only within that enclosure; but in gospel-times the mountains and hills of the Gentile world shall be enriched with these privileges by the gospel of Christ preached, and professed, and received in the power of it. When great multitudes were converted to the faith of Christ, and nations were born at once, when the preachers of the gospel were <hi type="italic">always caused to triumph in</hi> the success of their preaching, then the <hi type="italic">ploughman overtook the reaper;</hi> and when, the Gentile churches were <hi type="italic">enriched in all utterance, and in all knowledge,</hi> and all manner of <hi type="italic">spiritual gifts</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.5">1 Cor. i. 5</reference>), then the <hi type="italic">mountains dropped sweet wine.</hi> <div eID="gen20258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20259" type="x-p"/> IV. That the kingdom of the Messiah shall be well peopled; as the country shall be replenished, so shall the cities be; there shall be mouths for this meat, <reference osisRef="Amos.9.14">v. 14</reference>. Those that were carried captives shall be brought back out of their captivity; their enemies shall not be able to detain them in the land of their captivity, nor shall they themselves incline to settle in it, but the remnant shall return, and shall <hi type="italic">build the waste cities and inhabit them,</hi> shall form themselves into Christian churches and set up pure doctrine, worship, and discipline among them, according to the gospel charter, by which Christ's cities are incorporated; and they shall enjoy the benefit and comfort thereof; they shall <hi type="italic">plant vineyards,</hi> and <hi type="italic">make gardens.</hi> Though the mountains and hills drop wine, and the privileges of the gospel-church are laid in common, yet they shall enclose for themselves, not to monopolize these privileges, to the exclusion of others, but to appropriate and improve these privileges, in communion with others, and they shall <hi type="italic">drink the wine,</hi> and <hi type="italic">eat the fruit,</hi> of their own <hi type="italic">vineyards and gardens;</hi> for those that take pains in religion, as men must do about their vineyards and gardens, shall have both the pleasure and profit of it. The <hi type="italic">bringing again</hi> of the <hi type="italic">captivity</hi> of God's Israel, which is here promised, may refer to the cancelling of the ceremonial law, which had been long to God's Israel as a <hi type="italic">yoke of bondage,</hi> and the investing of them in the liberty wherewith Christ came to make his church free, <reference osisRef="Gal.5.1">Gal. v. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen20259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20260" type="x-p"/> V. That the kingdom of the Messiah shall take such deep rooting in the world as never to be rooted out of it (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will plant them upon their land.</hi> God's spiritual Israel shall be planted by the right hand of God himself upon the land assigned them, and <hi type="italic">they shall no more be pulled up out of it,</hi> as the old Jewish church was. God will preserve them from throwing themselves out of it by a total apostasy, and will preserve them from being thrown out of it by malice of their enemies; the church may be corrupted, but shall not quite forsake God, may be persecuted, but shall not quite be forsaken of God, so that the gates of hell, neither with their temptations nor with their terrors, shall prevail against it. Two things secure the perpetuity of the church:—1. God's grants to it: It <hi type="italic">is the land which I have given them;</hi> and God will confirm and maintain his own grants. The part he has given to his people is that good part which shall never be taken from them; he will not revoke his grant, and all the powers of earth and hell shall not invalidate it. 2. Its interest in him: He is <hi type="italic">the Lord thy God,</hi> who has said it, and will make it good, <hi type="italic">thine, O Israel!</hi> who shall <hi type="italic">reign for ever</hi> as thine <hi type="italic">unto all generations.</hi> And because he lives the church shall live also.  <chapter eID="Amos.9"/> <div eID="gen20260" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen20074" osisID="Amos" type="book"/>

entries.9e4e5fca957b8c8bc4187c0bcd5900ffea4b8b8b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12633"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 9</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Amos.9.1-Amos.9.15">Am 9:1-15</reference>. Fifth and Last Vision.</title> <div sID="gen23318" type="x-p"/> None can escape the coming judgment in any hiding-place: for God is omnipresent and irresistible (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.1-Amos.9.6">Am 9:1-6</reference>). As a kingdom, Israel shall perish as if it never was in covenant with Him: but as individuals the house of Jacob shall not utterly perish, nay, not one of the least of the righteous shall fall, but only all the sinners (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.7-Amos.9.10">Am 9:7-10</reference>). Restoration of the Jews finally to their own land after the re-establishment of the fallen tabernacle of David; consequent conversion of all the heathen (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.11-Amos.9.15">Am 9:11-15</reference>).<div eID="gen23318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23319" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12633"/><hi type="bold">1. Lord ... upon the altar--</hi>namely, in the idolatrous temple at Beth-el; the calves which were spoken of in <reference osisRef="Amos.8.14">Am 8:14</reference>. Hither they would flee for protection from the Assyrians, and would perish in the ruins, with the vain object of their trust [Henderson]. Jehovah stands here to direct the destruction of it, them, and the idolatrous nation. He demands many victims on the altar, but they are to be human victims. Calvin and Fairbairn, and others, make it in the temple at Jerusalem. Judgment was to descend both on Israel and Judah. As the services of both alike ought to have been offered on the Jerusalem temple-altar, it is there that Jehovah ideally stands, as if the whole people were assembled there, their abominations lying unpardoned there, and crying for vengeance, though in fact committed elsewhere (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.1-Ezek.8.18">Eze 8:1-18</reference>). This view harmonizes with the similarity of the vision in Amos to that in <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1-Isa.6.13">Is 6:1-13</reference>, at Jerusalem. Also with the end of this chapter (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.11-Amos.9.15">Am 9:11-15</reference>), which applies both to Judah and Israel: "the tabernacle of David," namely, at Jerusalem. His attitude, "standing," implies fixity of purpose.<div eID="gen23319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23320" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lintel--</hi>rather, the sphere-like capital of the column [Maurer].<div eID="gen23320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23321" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">posts--</hi>rather, "thresholds," as in <reference osisRef="Isa.6.4">Is 6:4</reference>, Margin. The temple is to be smitten below as well as above, to ensure utter destruction.<div eID="gen23321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23322" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cut them in the head--</hi>namely, with the broken fragments of the capitals and columns (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.68.21">Psa 68:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.3.13">Ha 3:13</reference>).<div eID="gen23322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23323" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">slay the last of them--</hi>their posterity [Henderson]. The survivors [Maurer]. Jehovah's directions are addressed to His angels, ministers of judgment (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.1-Ezek.9.11">Eze 9:1-11</reference>).<div eID="gen23323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23324" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that fleeth ... shall not flee away--</hi>He who fancies himself safe and out of reach of the enemy shall be taken (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.14">Am 2:14</reference>). <div eID="gen23324" type="x-p"/>
entries.2d097c5d20ff3f31fe2333bdcde2026851512e38: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12634"/><div sID="gen23325" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12634"/><hi type="bold">2. Though they dig into hell--</hi>though they hide ever so deeply in the earth (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.8">Psa 139:8</reference>).<div eID="gen23325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23326" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">though they climb up to heaven--</hi>though they ascend the greatest heights (<reference osisRef="Job.20.6">Job 20:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.20.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.53">Jr 51:53</reference>; Ob 4). <div eID="gen23326" type="x-p"/>
entries.050d34cb7ab3968700abccaccb8e676fce4336ea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12635"/><div sID="gen23327" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12635"/><hi type="bold">3. Carmel--</hi>where the forests, and, on the west side, the caves, furnished hiding-places (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.2">Am 1:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.6.2">Jud 6:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.6">1Sa 13:6</reference>).<div eID="gen23327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23328" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the sea--</hi>the Mediterranean, which flows at the foot of Mount Carmel; forming a strong antithesis to it.<div eID="gen23328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23329" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">command the serpent--</hi>the sea-serpent, a term used for any great water monster (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Is 27:1</reference>). The symbol of cruel and oppressive kings (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.13">Psa 74:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.14">14</reference>). <div eID="gen23329" type="x-p"/>
entries.8b55d39cef89d4611bd45774df2eaf8145066316: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12636"/><div sID="gen23330" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12636"/><hi type="bold">4. though they go into captivity--</hi>hoping to save their lives by voluntarily surrendering to the foe. <div eID="gen23330" type="x-p"/>
entries.b1dc42b24b694a8c112c22f5e1b0496dc68fa2ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12637"/><div sID="gen23331" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12637"/>5. As Amos had threatened that nowhere should the Israelites be safe from the divine judgments, he here shows God's omnipotent ability to execute His threats. So in the case of the threat in <reference osisRef="Amos.8.8">Am 8:8</reference>, God is here stated to be the first cause of the mourning of "all that dwell" in the land, and of its rising "like a flood, and of its being "drowned, as by the flood of Egypt." <div eID="gen23331" type="x-p"/>
entries.f3e5fc89dc7c38ce2ec9cdaf7bad8209890f3ba1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12638"/><div sID="gen23332" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12638"/><hi type="bold">6. stories--</hi>literally, "ascents," that is, upper chambers, to which the ascent is by steps [Maurer]; evidently referring to the words in <reference osisRef="Ps.104.3">Psa 104:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.13">13</reference>. Grotius explains it, God's royal throne, expressed in language drawn from Solomon's throne, to which the ascent was by steps (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.18">1Ki 10:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.19">19</reference>).<div eID="gen23332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23333" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">founded his troop--</hi>namely, all animate creatures, which are God's troop, or host (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.1">Ge 2:1</reference>), doing His will (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.20">Psa 103:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.103.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.11">Joe 2:11</reference>). Maurer translates, "His vault," that is, the vaulted sky, which seems to rest on the earth supported by the horizon. <div eID="gen23333" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae659dd81662fd927c3ee656a9404e1e29f2c9b3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12639"/><div sID="gen23334" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12639"/><hi type="bold">7. unto me--</hi>however great ye seem to yourselves. Do not rely on past privileges, and on My having delivered you from Egypt, as if therefore I never would remove you from Canaan. I make no more account of you than of "the Ethiopian" (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.13.23">Jr 13:23</reference>). "Have not I (who) brought you out of Egypt," done as much for other peoples? For instance, did I not bring "the Philistines (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.14.29">Is 14:29</reference>, &c.) from Caphtor (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.2.23">De 2:23</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Jer.47.4">Jr 47:4</reference>), where they had been bond-servants, and the Syrians from Kir?" It is appropriate, that as the Syrians migrated into Syria from Kir (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Isa.22.6">Is 22:6</reference>), so they should be carried back captive into the same land (see on <reference osisRef="Amos.1.15">Am 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.9">2Ki 16:9</reference>), just as elsewhere Israel is threatened with a return to Egypt whence they had been delivered. The "Ethiopians," Hebrew, "Cushites," were originally akin to the race that founded Babylon: the cuneiform inscriptions in this confirming independently the Scripture statement (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.6">Ge 10:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.8.10">8, 10</reference>). <div eID="gen23334" type="x-p"/>
entries.8ee9098ab5b767945a95b293657da1e07dfb08aa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12640"/><div sID="gen23335" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12640"/><hi type="bold">8. eyes ... upon the sinful kingdom--</hi>that is, I am watching all its sinful course in order to punish it (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.9.4">Am 9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.34.15">Psa 34:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.16">16</reference>).<div eID="gen23335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23336" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not utterly destroy the house of Jacob--</hi>Though as a "kingdom" the nation is now utterly to perish, a remnant is to be spared for "Jacob," their forefather's sake (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.30.11">Jr 30:11</reference>); to fulfil the covenant whereby "the seed of Israel" is hereafter to be "a nation for ever" (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.36">Jr 31:36</reference>). <div eID="gen23336" type="x-p"/>
entries.0ed76a9f5e7e77ef38df1453ca586d8cce0dc57f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12641"/><div sID="gen23337" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12641"/><hi type="bold">9. sift--</hi>I will cause the Israelites to be tossed about through all nations as corn is shaken about in a sieve, in such a way, however, that while the chaff and dust (the wicked) fall through (perish), all the solid grains (the godly elect) remain (are preserved), (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Ro 11:26</reference>; compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Jer.3.14">Jr 3:14</reference>). So spiritual Israel's final safety is ensured (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.32">Lu 22:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.28">Joh 10:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.6.39">6:39</reference>). <div eID="gen23337" type="x-p"/>
entries.56ca8ae45fbec93cf5bde577496220c336026ff7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12642"/><div sID="gen23338" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12642"/><hi type="bold">10. All the sinners--</hi>answering to the chaff in the image in <reference osisRef="Amos.9.9">Am 9:9</reference>, which falls on the earth, in opposition "to the grain" that does not "fall."<div eID="gen23338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23339" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">overtake ... us--</hi>"come on us from behind" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen23339" type="x-p"/>
entries.81e7ac05d198165b95c1a01eb9a7296dd53b94fa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12643"/><div sID="gen23340" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12643"/><hi type="bold">11. In that day--</hi>quoted by James (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.16">Ac 15:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.17">17</reference>), "After this," that is, in the dispensation of Messiah (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Ge 49:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.3.4">Ho 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.28">Joe 2:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.1">3:1</reference>).<div eID="gen23340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23341" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tabernacle of David--</hi>not "the house of David," which is used of his affairs when prospering (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.1">2Sa 3:1</reference>), but the tent or booth, expressing the low condition to which his kingdom and family had fallen in Amos' time, and subsequently at the Babylonian captivity before the restoration; and secondarily, in the last days preceding Israel's restoration under Messiah, the antitype to David (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.13">Psa 102:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.102.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.9">Jr 30:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.24">Eze 34:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.24">37:24</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Isa.12.1">Is 12:1</reference>). The type is taken from architecture (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.20">Ep 2:20</reference>). The restoration under Zerubbabel can only be a partial, temporary fulfilment; for it did not include Israel, which nation is the main subject of Amos' prophecies, but only Judah; also Zerubbabel's kingdom was not independent and settled; also all the prophets end their prophecies with Messiah, whose advent is the cure of all previous disorders. "Tabernacle" is appropriate to Him, as His human nature is the tabernacle which He assumed in becoming Immanuel, "God with us" (<reference osisRef="John.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference>). "Dwelt," literally, tabernacled "among us" (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.21.3">Re 21:3</reference>). Some understand "the tabernacle of David" as that which David pitched for the ark in Zion, after bringing it from Obed-edom's house. It remained there all his reign for thirty years, till the temple of Solomon was built, whereas the "tabernacle of the congregation" remained at Gibeon (<reference osisRef="2Chr.1.3">2Ch 1:3</reference>), where the priests ministered in sacrifices (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.39">1Ch 16:39</reference>). Song and praise was the service of David's attendants before the ark (Asaph, &c.): a type of the gospel separation between the sacrificial service (Messiah's priesthood now in heaven) and the access of believers on earth to the presence of God, apart from the former (compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.12-2Sam.6.17">2Sa 6:12-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.37-1Chr.16.39">1Ch 16:37-39</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.1.3">2Ch 1:3</reference>).<div eID="gen23341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23342" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">breaches thereof--</hi>literally, "of them," that is, of the whole nation, Israel as well as Judah.<div eID="gen23342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23343" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as in ... days of old--</hi>as it was formerly in the days of David and Solomon, when the kingdom was in its full extent and undivided. <div eID="gen23343" type="x-p"/>
entries.e12429250604d0cdbef3fedd9d5013252d483b2d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12644"/><div sID="gen23344" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12644"/><hi type="bold">12. That they may possess ... remnant of Edom, and of all the heathen--</hi>"Edom," the bitter foe, though the brother, of Israel; therefore to be punished (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.11">Am 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>), Israel shall be lord of the "remnant" of Edom left after the punishment of the latter. James quotes it, "That the residue of men might seek after the Lord, and all the Gentiles," &c. For "all the heathen" nations stand on the same footing as Edom: Edom is the representative of them all. The residue or remnant in both cases expresses those left after great antecedent calamities (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.27">Ro 9:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.16">Zec 14:16</reference>). Here the conversion of "all nations" (of which the earnest was given in James's time) is represented as only to be realized on the re-establishment of the theocracy under Messiah, the Heir of the throne of David (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.11">Am 9:11</reference>). The possession of the heathen nations by Israel is to be spiritual, the latter being the ministers to the former for their conversion to Messiah, King of the Jews; just as the first conversions of pagans were through the ministry of the apostles, who were Jews. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.54.3">Is 54:3</reference>, "thy seed shall inherit the Gentiles" (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.49.8">Is 49:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.4.13">Ro 4:13</reference>). A remnant of Edom became Jews under John Hyrcanus, and the rest amalgamated with the Arabians, who became Christians subsequently.<div eID="gen23344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23345" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which are called by my name--</hi>that is, who belong to Me, whom I claim as Mine (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.8">Psa 2:8</reference>); in the purposes of electing grace, God terms them already called by His name. Compare the title, "the children," applied by anticipation, <reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">He 2:14</reference>. Hence as an act of sovereign grace, fulfilling His promise, it is spoken of God. Proclaim His title as sovereign, "the Lord that doeth this" ("all these things," <reference osisRef="Acts.15.17">Ac 15:17</reference>, namely, all these and such like acts of sovereign love). <div eID="gen23345" type="x-p"/>
entries.a4cee332101c61f71b5905d0bf231c18e8806cc5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12645"/><div sID="gen23346" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12645"/><hi type="bold">13. the days come--</hi>at the future restoration of the Jews to their own land.<div eID="gen23346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23347" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ploughman shall overtake ... reaper ... treader of grapes him that soweth--</hi>fulfilling <reference osisRef="Lev.26.5">Le 26:5</reference>. Such shall be the abundance that the harvest and vintage can hardly be gathered before the time for preparing for the next crop shall come. Instead of the greater part of the year being spent in war, the whole shall be spent in sowing and reaping the fruits of earth. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.65.21-Isa.65.23">Is 65:21-23</reference>, as to the same period.<div eID="gen23347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23348" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">soweth seed--</hi>literally, "draweth it forth," namely, from the sack in order to sow it.<div eID="gen23348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23349" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mountains ... drop sweet wine--</hi>an appropriate image, as the vines in Palestine were trained on terraces at the sides of the hills. <div eID="gen23349" type="x-p"/>
entries.5bc3e0510c810801983e90d1e1ddec4c801a4f10: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12646"/><div sID="gen23350" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12646"/><hi type="bold">14. build the waste cities--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.61.4">Is 61:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.33-Ezek.36.36">Eze 36:33-36</reference>). <div eID="gen23350" type="x-p"/>
entries.19f82a1df4cf5aa9d29366f86c55fb75a31062a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12647"/><div sID="gen23351" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12647"/><hi type="bold">15. plant them ... no more be pulled up--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.32.41">Jr 32:41</reference>).<div eID="gen23351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23352" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy God--</hi>Israel's; this is the ground of their restoration, God's original choice of them as His. <chapter eID="Amos.9"/><div eID="gen23352" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen22992" osisID="Amos" type="book"/>

entries.d5b99e299b43bd447539ee466a91f377aa7462c7: <div eID="gen34475" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen34476" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34477" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34477" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34476" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34478" type="x-p"/> The first part of this chapter contains another vision, in which God is represented as declaring the final ruin of the kingdom of Israel, and the general dispersion of the people, <reference osisRef="Amo.9.1-Amo.9.10">Amo 9:1-10</reference>. The prophet then passes to the great blessedness of the people of God under the Gospel dispensation, <reference osisRef="Amo.9.11-Amo.9.15">Amo 9:11-15</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Act.15.15">Act 15:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.15.16">Act 15:16</reference>. <div eID="gen34478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34479" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen34479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34480" type="x-p"/> I saw the Lord standing upon the altar - As this is a continuation of the preceding prophecy, the altar here may be one of those either at Dan or Beer-sheba. <div eID="gen34480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34481" type="x-p"/> Smite the lintel - Either the piece of timber that binds the wall above the door, or the upper part of the door frame, in which the cheeks, or side posts, are inserted, and which corresponds to the threshold, or lower part of the door frame. <div eID="gen34481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34482" type="x-p"/> And cut them in the head - Let all the lintels of all the doors of all those temples be thus cut, as a sign that the whole shall be thrown down and totally demolished. Or this may refer to their heads - chief men, who were principals in these transgressions. Mark their temples, their priests, their prophets, and their princes, for destruction. <div eID="gen34482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34483" type="x-p"/> He that fleeth - shall not flee away - He shall be caught before he can get out of the reach of danger. <div eID="gen34483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34484" type="x-p"/> And he that escapeth (that makes good his flight) shall not be delivered - Captivity, famine, or sword, shall reach him even there.
entries.32e910c1fc502398a4c8b55ab5ce7570d08e4b68: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen34484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34485" type="x-p"/> Though they dig into hell - Though they should get into the deepest caverns; though they climb up to heaven - get to the most inaccessible heights; I will drag them up from the one, and pull them down from the other.
entries.f2392037cee9272b078aa75463526a73192eb398: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen34485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34486" type="x-p"/> Though they hide themselves - All these are metaphorical expressions, to show the impossibility of escape.
entries.4e2f838d510023f6abb4c1e774507c9b8e145296: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen34486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34487" type="x-p"/> I will set mine eyes upon them for evil - I will use that very providence against them which before worked for their good. Should they look upward, they shall see nothing but the terrible lightning-like eye of a sin-avenging God.
entries.4a843509e5f007ce05b81a3a4efea4a806030270: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen34487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34488" type="x-p"/> The Lord God of hosts is he - So powerful is he that a touch of his hand shall melt or dissolve the land, and cause all its inhabitants to mourn. Here is still a reference to the earthquake. See the note <reference osisRef="Amo.8.8">Amo 8:8</reference>, where the same images are used.
entries.f692bddff18df1efde4928b5d66bfebad0fa2484: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen34488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34489" type="x-p"/> Buildeth his stories in the heaven - There is here an allusion to large houses, where there are cellars, or places dug in the ground as repositories for corn; middle apartments, or stories, for the families to live in; and the house-top for persons to take the air upon. There may be here a reference to the various systems which God has formed in illimitable space, transcending each other, as the planets do in our solar system: and thus we find Solomon speaking when addressing the Most High: "The heavens and the heaven of heavens cannot contain thee, השמים ושמי השמים hashshamayim ushemey hashshamayim, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.27">1Kgs 8:27</reference>. Six heavens are necessarily implied in these three words. According to the points, the first and third are in the dual number, and the second is the contracted form of the plural. But how many more spheres may be intended who can tell? There may be millions of millions of stellar systems in unlimited space; and then what are all these to the Vast Immensity of God! <div eID="gen34489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34490" type="x-p"/> Hath founded his troop in the earth - אגדיו aguddatho, from אגד agad, to bind or gather together, possibly meaning the seas and other collections of waters which he has gathered together and bound by his perpetual decree, that they cannot pass; yet when he calleth for these very waters, as in the general deluge, he "poureth them out upon the face of the earth." <div eID="gen34490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34491" type="x-p"/> The Lord is his name - This points out his infinite essence. But what is that essence? and what is his nature? and what his immensity and eternity? What archangel can tell?
entries.90effff805de6f7ed11ad2d943061cd5fea250c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen34491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34492" type="x-p"/> Children of the Ethiopians - Or Cushites. Cush was the son of Ham, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.6">Gen 10:6</reference>; and his descendants inhabited a part of Arabia Petraea and Arabia Felix. All this stock was universally despised. See Bochart. <div eID="gen34492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34493" type="x-p"/> The Philistines from Caphtor - The island of Crete, the people of which were the Cherethim. See, <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.14">1Sam 30:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.25.16">Eze 25:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zep.2.5">Zep 2:5</reference>. <div eID="gen34493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34494" type="x-p"/> The Syrians from Kir? - Perhaps a city of the Medes, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.6">Isa 22:6</reference>. Aram, from whom Syria had its name, was the son of Shem, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.22">Gen 10:22</reference>. Part of his descendants settled in this city, and part in Aram Naharaim, "Syria of the two rivers," viz., Mesopotamia, included between the Tigris and the Euphrates. <div eID="gen34494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34495" type="x-p"/> The meaning of the verse is this: Do not presume on my having brought you out of the land of Egypt and house of bondage, into a land flowing with milk and honey. I have brought other nations, and some of your neighbors, who are your enemies, from comparatively barren countries, into fruitful territories; such, for instance, as the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir.
entries.b55887055ac9aacde3d6b35a34d3720ab9219750: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen34495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34496" type="x-p"/> The eyes of the Lord God are upon the sinful kingdom - The kingdom of Israel, peculiarly sinful; and therefore to be signally destroyed by the Assyrians. <div eID="gen34496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34497" type="x-p"/> I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob - The race shall not become extinct: I will reserve them as monuments of my justice, and finally of my mercy.
entries.30f6069fdb565fd0da354c5320180f78dd675610: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen34497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34498" type="x-p"/> I will sift the house of Israel among all nations - I will disperse them over the face of the earth; and yet I will so order it that the good shall not be lost; for though they shall be mixed among distant nations, yet there shall be a general restoration of them to their own land. <div eID="gen34498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34499" type="x-p"/> The least grain - צרור tseror, little stone, pebble, or gravel. Not one of them, howsoever little or contemptible, when the time comes, shall be left behind. All shall be collected in Christ, and brought into their own land.
entries.75864399806ef420a56e7a2fd849acf75ef8cb33: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen34499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34500" type="x-p"/> All the sinners of my people - Those who are the boldest and most incredulous; especially they who despise my warnings, and say the evil day shall not overtake nor prevent us; they shall die by the sword. It is no evidence of a man's safety that he is presumptuously fearless. There is a blessing to him who trembles at God's word.
entries.78bcfd2ac1b535312502b5483e0b13ceedd5d590: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen34500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34501" type="x-p"/> Will I raise up the tabernacle of David - It is well known that the kingdom of Israel, the most profane and idolatrous, fell first, and that the kingdom of Judah continued long after, and enjoyed considerable prosperity under Hezekiah and Josiah. The remnant of the Israelites that were left by the Assyrians became united to the kingdom of Judah; and of the others, many afterwards joined them: but this comparatively short prosperity and respite, previously to the Babylonish captivity, could not be that, as Calmet justly observes, which is mentioned here. This could not be called closing up the breaches, raising up the ruins, and building it as in the days of old; nor has any state of this kind taken place since; and, consequently, the prophecy remains to be fulfilled. It must therefore refer to their restoration under the Gospel, when they shall receive the Lord Jesus as their Messiah, and be by him restored to their own land. See these words quoted by James, <reference osisRef="Act.15.17">Act 15:17</reference>. Then indeed it is likely that they shall possess the remnant of Edom, and have the whole length and breadth of Immanuel's land, <reference osisRef="Amo.9.12">Amo 9:12</reference>. Nor can it be supposed that the victories gained by the Asmoneans could be that intended by the prophet and which he describes in such lofty terms. These victories procured only a short respite, and a very imperfect re-establishment of the tabernacle of David; and could not warrant the terms of the prediction in these verses.
entries.7b5214f6cf1424d3ef3ec1776d3a710a7223c493: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen34501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34502" type="x-p"/> That they may possess the remnant of Edom - Bp. Newcome translates this clause as follows: "That the residue of men may seek Jehovah, and all the heathen who are called by my name." Here, instead of אדום Edom, he reads אדם Adam, men or mankind, which is the reading of the Arabic, and some MSS. of the Syriac, and of <reference osisRef="Act.15.17">Act 15:17</reference>. <div eID="gen34502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34503" type="x-p"/> The Pachomian MS. of the Septuagint adds here, ὁπως εκζητησωσι με, that they may seek me. And the Arabic has the Lord; and in stead of יירשו yireshu, "they shall possess," the learned bishop seems to have read ידרשו yidreshu, "they may seek;" and thus the text resembles the quotation by St. James, <reference osisRef="Act.15.17">Act 15:17</reference>, "That the residue of men might seek after the Lord." It is strange that not one of the MSS. collated by Kennicott and De Rossi, nor any of my own, favors or countenances any of these alterations. I am of opinion, therefore, that we must dismiss all these conjectural emendations, and take the Hebrew text as we find it. That it speaks of the conversion of the Jews in Gospel times, we have the authority of the New Testament as above to prove; and it we cannot make the words, as they stand there, entirely to agree with the words here, the subject is not affected by it. The Jews shall be converted and restored, and this text in both covenants is a proof of it.
entries.2392cda08e14385355df6fa7d8f9e6a79aecb737: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen34503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34504" type="x-p"/> The ploughman shall overtake the reaper - All the seasons shall succeed in due and natural order: but the crops shall be so copious in the fields and in the vineyards, that a long time shall be employed in gathering and disposing of them; so that the seasons of ploughing, sowing, gathering the grapes, treading the wine-press, etc., shall press on the heels of each other; so vast will be the abundance, and so long the time necessary to gather and cure the grain and fruits. We are informed by travelers in the Holy Land, Barbary, etc., that the vintage at Aleppo lasts from the fifteenth of September to the middle of November; and that the sowing season begins at the close of October, and lasts through all November. Here, then, the ploughman, sower, grape-gatherer, and operator at the wine-press, not only succeed each other, but have parts of these operations going on at the same time. But great fertility in the land, abundance in the crops, and regularity of the seasons, seem to be the things which the prophet especially predicts. These are all poetical and prophetical images, by which happy times are pointed out.
entries.fb067f66f6f74b78dedf10472be88def66a3141b: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen34504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34505" type="x-p"/> They shall plant vineyards, and drink the wine - When threatened with great evils, <reference osisRef="Amo.5.11">Amo 5:11</reference>, it is said, "They shall plant pleasant vineyards but shall not drink the wine of them." Previously to their restoration, they shall labor for others; after their restoration, they shall labor for themselves.
entries.71ba86a051c3d429fa8da56c4ef4ceec4a0c2081: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen34505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34506" type="x-p"/> I will plant them upon their land - They shall receive a permanent establishment there. <div eID="gen34506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34507" type="x-p"/> And they shall no more be pulled up - Most certainly this prophecy has never yet been fulfilled. They were pulled out by the Assyrian captivity, and by that of Babylon. Many were planted in again, and again pulled out by the Roman conquest and captivity, and were never since planted in, but are now scattered among all the nations of the earth. I conclude, as the word of God cannot fail, and this has not yet been fulfilled, it therefore follows that it will and must be fulfilled to the fullness of its spirit and intention. And this is established by the conclusion: "Saith the Lord thy God." He is Jehovah, and cannot fail; he is Thy God, and will do it. He can do it, because he is Jehovah; and he will do it, because he is Thy God. Amen.  <chapter eID="Amos.9"/> <div eID="gen34507" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen34189" osisID="Amos" type="book"/>

entries.abfe3b038bd2829ffb95c244485747b8ba05897a: <reference osisRef="Amos.9.1">Amo 9:1</reference> <hi type="italic">“I saw the Lord standing by the altar; and He said, Smite the top, that the thresholds may tremble, and smash them upon the head of all of them; and I will slay their remnant with the sword: a fugitive of them shall not flee; and an escaped one of them shall not escape.” </hi> The correct and full interpretation not only of this verse, but of the whole chapter, depends upon the answer to be given to the question, what altar we are to understand by <hi type="italic">hammizbēăch</hi>. Ewald, Hitzig, Hofmann, and Baur follow Cyril in thinking of the temple at Bethel, because, as Hitzig says, this vision attaches itself in an explanatory manner to the close of <reference osisRef="Amos.8.14">Amo 8:14</reference>, and because, according to Hofmann, “if the word of the prophet in general was directed against the kingdom, the royal house and the sanctuary of the ten tribes, the article before <hi type="italic">hammizbēăch</hi> points to the altar of the sanctuary in the kingdom of Israel, to the altar at Bethel, against which he has already prophesied in a perfectly similar manner in Amo 3:14.” But there is no ground whatever for the assertion that our vision contains simply an explanation of Amo 8:14. The connection with <reference osisRef="Amos.8.1-Amos.8.14">Amo 8:1-14</reference> is altogether not so close, that the object of the prophecy in the one chapter must of necessity cover that of the other. And it is quite incorrect to say that the word of the prophet throughout is directed simply against the kingdom of the ten tribes, or that, although Amos does indeed reprove the sins of Judah as well as those of Israel, he proclaims destruction to the kingdom of Jeroboam alone. As early as <reference osisRef="Amos.2.5">Amo 2:5</reference> he announces desolation to Judah by fire, and the burning of the palaces of Jerusalem; and in <reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Amo 6:1</reference>, again, he gives utterance to a woe upon the self-secure in Zion, as well as upon the careless ones in Samaria. And lastly, it is evident from <reference osisRef="Amos.9.8-Amos.9.10">Amo 9:8-10</reference> of the present chapter, that the sinful kingdom which is to be destroyed from the face of the earth is not merely the kingdom of the ten tribes, but the kingdoms of Judah and Israel, which are embraced in one. For although it is stated immediately afterwards that the Lord will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob, but will shake the house of Israel among all nations, the house of Jacob cannot mean the kingdom of Judah, and the house of Israel the kingdom of the ten tribes, because such a contrast between Judah and Israel makes the thought too lame, and the antithesis between the destruction of the sinful kingdom and the utter destruction of the nation is quite obliterated. Amos does not generally draw such a distinction between the house of Jacob and the house of Israel, as that the first represents Judah, and the second the ten tribes; but he uses the two epithets as synonymous, as we may see from a comparison of <reference osisRef="Amos.6.8">Amo 6:8</reference> with <reference osisRef="Amos.6.14">Amo 6:14</reference>, where the rejection of the pride of Israel and the hating of its palaces (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.8">Amo 9:8</reference>) are practically interpreted by the raising up of a nation which oppresses the house of Israel in all its borders (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.14">Amo 9:14</reference>). And so also in the chapter before us, the “house of Israel” (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.9">Amo 9:9</reference>) is identical with “Israel” and the “children of Israel” (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.7">Amo 9:7</reference>), whom God brought up out of Egypt. But God brought up out of Egypt not the ten tribes, but the twelve. And consequently it is decidedly incorrect to restrict the contents of <reference osisRef="Amos.9.1-Amos.9.10">Amo 9:1-10</reference> to the kingdom of the ten tribes. And if this be the case, we cannot possibly understand by <hi type="italic">hammizbēăch</hi> in <reference osisRef="Amos.9.1">Amo 9:1</reference> the altar of Bethel, especially seeing that not only does Amos foretel the visitation or destruction of the <hi type="italic">altars</hi> of Bethel in <reference osisRef="Amos.3.14">Amo 3:14</reference>, and therefore recognises not one altar only in Bethel, but a plurality of altars, but that he also speaks in <reference osisRef="Amos.7.9">Amo 7:9</reference> of the desolation of the high places and sanctuaries in Israel, and in <reference osisRef="Amos.8.14">Amo 8:14</reference> places the sanctuary at Daniel on a par with that at Bethel; so that there was not any <hi type="italic">one</hi> altar in the kingdom of the ten tribes, which could be called <hi type="italic">hammizbēăch</hi>, the altar <hi type="italic">par excellence</hi>, inasmuch as it possessed from the very beginning two sanctuaries of equal dignity (viz., at Bethel and Dan). <hi type="italic">Hammizbēăch</hi>, therefore, both here and at <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.2">Eze 9:2</reference>, is the altar of burnt-offering in the temple, at Jerusalem, the sanctuary of the whole of the covenant nation, to which even the ten bribes still belonged, in spite of their having fallen away from the house of David. So long as the Lord still continued to send prophets to the ten tribes, so long did they pass as still forming part of the people of God, and so long also was the temple at Jerusalem the divinely appointed sanctuary and the throne of Jehovah, from which both blessings and punishment issued from the. The Lord roars from Zion, and from Zion He utters His voice (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.2">Amo 1:2</reference>), not only upon the nations who have shown hostility to Judah or Israel, but also upon Judah and Israel, on account of their departure from His law (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.4">Amo 2:4</reference> and Amo 2:6.). <div eID="gen16422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16423" type="x-p"/> The vision in this verse is founded upon the idea that the whole nation is assembled before the Lord at the threshold of the temple, so that it is buried under the ruins of the falling building, in consequence of the blow upon the top, which shatters the temple to its very foundations. The Lord appears at the altar, because here at the sacrificial place of the nation the sins of Israel are heaped up, that He may execute judgment upon the nation there. נצּב על, standing at (not upon) the altar, as in 1Ki 13:1. He gives commandment to smite the top. The person who is to do this is not mentioned; but it was no doubt an angel, probably the המּלאך המּשׁחית, who brought the pestilence as a punishment at the numbering of the people in the time of David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.24.15-2Sam.24.16">2Sa 24:15-16</reference>), who smote the army of the Assyrian king Sennacherib before Jerusalem (2Ki 19:35), and who also slew the first-born of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.13">Exo 12:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.23">Exo 12:23</reference>); whereas in <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.2">Eze 9:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.7">Eze 9:7</reference>, He is represented as accomplishing the judgment of destruction by means of six angels. <hi type="italic">Hakkaphtōr</hi>, the knob or top; in <reference osisRef="Exod.25.31">Exo 25:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.25.33">Exo 25:33</reference>, ff., an ornament upon the shaft and branches of the golden candlestick. Here it is an ornament at the top of the columns, and not “the lintel of the door,” or “the pinnacle of the temple with its ornaments.” For the latter explanation of <hi type="italic">kaphtōr</hi>, which cannot be philologically sustained, by no means follows from the fact that the antithesis to the <hi type="italic">kaphtōr</hi> is formed by the <hi type="italic">sippı̄m</hi>, or thresholds of the door. The knob and threshold simply express the contrast between the loftiest summit and the lowest base, without at all warranting the conclusion that the <hi type="italic">saph</hi> denotes the base of the pillar which culminated in a knob, or <hi type="italic">kaphtōr</hi>, the top of the door which rested upon a threshold.
